Logistic Regression

In this section, we try to predict if a person has a coronary heart disease.

Logistic Regression Without Using Weights

I ignored the various weights in the dataset because I couldn’t figure out what they meant and how to use them. To my surprise, ignoring weights results in models that have ROC = 5.While writing this document, I found out that the previous sentence was wrong. My models were bad because of a bug. In my original code, I intended to train data on the training set that was not defined in the script, and was using another dataframe called train from the global environment. After correcting the bug, the ROC looks normal.

I tried to use high_density_level,low_density_level,triglyceride_level as variables. This model didn’t work.

# -----model with multiple predictors-----------.
# 1. Fit on training set
model <- glm(
  coronary ~ high_density_level + low_density_level + triglyceride_level,
  family = binomial,
  data = train
)

# 2. Predict on *validation* set
validation$prob <- predict(
  model,
  newdata = validation,
  type = "response"
)

# 3. ROC on validation set

g <- roc(response = validation$coronary,
         predictor = validation$prob)
## Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
## Setting direction: controls < cases
g
## 
## Call:
## roc.default(response = validation$coronary, predictor = validation$prob)
## 
## Data: validation$prob in 961 controls (validation$coronary 0) < 60 cases (validation$coronary 1).
## Area under the curve: 0.7247
plot(g)

Logistic Regression With Weights

After the previous trials, I realized the importance of the weights and decided to use them? but how? In order to learn how to use them, I studied NAHNAES’s sample design, a concept that I haven’t studied before and struggled to understand. After having an rudimentary understanding of its sample design, the next challenge is how to choose a weight since there are many weights in the dataset. It took me a while to understand the criteria - choose the weight for the smallest subsample if multiple subsamples are used in the analysis. In my case, I have decide which subsample is smaller because I have two: the phlebotomy subsample(people who gave blood specimen) and the fasting subsample (people who are asked to fast). It took me several hours just to decide on this. Finally, I realized that fasting subsample is smaller because they fasted first and then gave blood specimen. Then, I proceeded to use the fasting weight but the models couldn’t converge. After some trials, I used the phlebotomy weight, which finally worked.

Logistic Regression With Using Weight_2(Fasting Subsample Weight)

According to NHANES analytic guideline, this weight should be used. However, using fasting weight causes the model fail to converge. The exact reason of the failure requires further study.

Trying to fit a model with 3 predictors. This model won’t converge.

  design = design_sub,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

  design = design_sub_2,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

Logistic Regression With Using Weight_1(Phlebotomy Subsample Weight)

Since the previous method fails, the Phlebotomy weight is used since it is the weight for the second smallest subsample.

Logistic Regression With Using Weight_1 and Two Predictors

We fit a model using high_density_level and low_density_level.

# --------- model with two predictors -----------------------
# train model on the train set
model <- svyglm(
  coronary ~ high_density_level +low_density_level ,
  design = design_train_sub,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

summary(model)
## 
## Call:
## svyglm(formula = coronary ~ high_density_level + low_density_level, 
##     design = design_train_sub, family = quasibinomial())
## 
## Survey design:
## subset(design_train, !is.na(coronary) & !is.na(high_density_level) & 
##     !is.na(low_density_level))
## 
## Coefficients:
##                     Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)         0.405189   0.471617   0.859 0.405823    
## high_density_level -0.008720   0.010009  -0.871 0.399413    
## low_density_level  -0.032348   0.006994  -4.625 0.000475 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for quasibinomial family taken to be 1.326199)
## 
## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 7
# predict on the validation set.

val_df <- design_validation_sub$variables
val_df$predicted <- predict(model, newdata = val_df, type = "response")

roc_val_both <- roc(
  response = val_df$coronary,
  predictor = val_df$predicted,
  weights = val_df$weight_1
)
## Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
## Setting direction: controls < cases
roc_val_both
## 
## Call:
## roc.default(response = val_df$coronary, predictor = val_df$predicted,     weights = val_df$weight_1)
## 
## Data: val_df$predicted in 970 controls (val_df$coronary 0) < 59 cases (val_df$coronary 1).
## Area under the curve: 0.7521
plot(roc_val_both)

From this model, we choose a threshhold that yields the highest accuracy.

# 1.choose the best threshold for this model and calculate the accuracy. 

roc_obj <- roc(response = val_df$coronary, predictor = val_df$predicted)
## Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
## Setting direction: controls < cases
best <- coords(roc_obj, "best", best.method="closest.topleft")
best
##   threshold specificity sensitivity
## 1 0.0497915         0.7   0.6949153
best_threshold <- as.numeric(best$threshold)

# 2. predicted classes using optimal threshold
val_df$predicted_labels <- ifelse(val_df$predicted >= best_threshold[], 1, 0)

# 3. accuracy
accuracy <- mean(val_df$predicted_labels == val_df$coronary)
accuracy
## [1] 0.6997085
